HINT TO THE NEW PARLIAMENT. Our parliaments have frequently had various sobriquets applied to them to denote the respective qualities by which they were distinguished. The last ought certainly to be known to posterity by the title of " the chattering parliament." It is curious to observe how the cacoethes loquendi has been of late years increasing in our legislature, especially in the popular portion of it. This is, probably, in a great degree attributable to the sad lack of men of commanding genius among our existing orators. When such highly gifted beings as Pitt, and Fox, and Burke, and Sheridan, and Wyndham, and Caming flourished, inferior minds did not venture to obtrude on the public attention. Debates were comparatively few in numher and after half a dozen of the principal speakers had expressed their opinions, the house would not listen to any others. But now (with rare exceptions) there is a dead level of mediocrity. Tom knows that lie can speak as well as Jack, and Bob knows that he can speak as well as Bill, and Dick knows that he can speak as well as Harry ; and so they all speak and keep one another in countenance. A more than feminine volubility prevails. With little or no preparation, an honourable gentleman starts up, and pours fourth an incoherent mass of matter in a style suited to the meridian of a parish vestry of a common hall. Talk, talk, talk, is the order of the day ; and it is never allowed to be a dropped order. One would think that our representatives had been study-
ing Matthews's " patter." Not a petition is presented but it is accompanied by one, two, three, ten, twenty speeches. If a hundred

vwmrosss: petitions are presented of the same description, the same speeches are repeated. Every topic is talked to tatters. First, we have the then the cold meat, then the hash, then subject is referred to the consideration of a committee above stairs, in which it undergoes ample and minute investigation : nevertheless, when the report is made to the house, it is debated with as much earnestness and prolixity as if the

before in the history world, there such persevering prattle. Beginning noon, at rarely, indeed, does it happen that an adjournment of the House of Commons take The consequence of all this is that little progress is made in real business ; and that measures of the highest public importance are necessarily postponed from time to time, until a period arrives when they must be either hurried through both houses in a crude and an imperfect state, or entirely abandoned. If some remedy be not devised for this enormous and growing evil, it will destroy all rational and wholesome legislation. With the change that has occurred in the character of the parliamentary debates, a corchange has, of course, occurred in the character of the parliamentary reporters. Those labours are much more severe, and much less agreeable than formerly. I he task, which was once one of instruction and delight' has become one of mere and disgust. although the size of the daily papers has been greatly increased, and the size of the types in which they are printed has been greatly diminished, yet that, in many instances, considerable curtailment and condensation necessarily take place in the reports ; the fac t being, that any approach to a verbatim report of a debate ol ten or twelve hours' duration would till two or three newspapers instead of one This brevity, however, is seldom or never to be lamented by the public, except when (as has recently been too frequently the case) questions of importance

are brought on at a late period of a night, the earlier portion of which has probably been wasted in frivolous and protracted conversations ; þÿ in "long galleries leading to nothing." þÿ Falmouth Packet.

FRIENDSHIP. Friendship, thou gift of Heavenly birth, Misused þÿ nay more þÿ profaned on earth ! Alas ! how common, yet how profaned, is the name of friend. The gamester, the spendthrift, the thoughtless man of pleasure, the mere possessor of fortune, nay þÿ even the drunkard and the sceptic, boast their friend. There is nothing so vile, nothing so despicable, but the term is applied to the associates in their vices or their follies. The giddy girl dignities the acquaintances she formed at school, which originated perhaps simply from their moving in the same society, or sharing equally in the gifts of fortune (for with the crowd intimacies are formed with no greater inducement), with the sacred name of friendship. But, how rare to find þÿ how valuablo when found a real friend! it is a jewel thrones þÿ cannot purchase. In the pride ol youth and happiness, we fancy all who seek our society are friends in heart as well as name; forgetful how many inducements may contribute to their attraction : we give pleasant parties, where they meet society which is agreeable to them, and which they could not enjoy elsewhere ; it

is in our power to procure them a ticket for the Opera or play ; a seat in a carriage is at their service at the races ; some have a manor over which it is pleasant to shoot in the game season ; others a house at some fashionable watering place, to which an invitation would not be disagreeable. Such may boast their dear three hundred friends ; but let all these advantages vanish, and the one flattered possessor be reduced to a state of comparative obscurity, as quickly will his friend disappear; and the name that was uttered bv every lip, and the form that was flattered by every tongue, will be as utterly forgotten as the flowers that ere while decked our hills and valleys, but have now given place to others of more brilliant hues þÿ Annette.

at>\ byron . The child of the late Lord Byron says a correspondent, is a lovely creature, now about eighteen years of age. I saw her the other day, each side of her temples was covered with many plaits of braided fine brown hair; her high arched brow, is a perfect model for a phrenologist ; and from what 1 have observi d of engravings, busts, &c. very much resembles her father, the late Lord Byron. To Newspaper Borrowers ! ! ! þÿ We have been thinking for some time past whether a slight hint to some of the gentry would not have a salutary effect. We have a large number of 'Headers of, and but very few Subscribers to the Gazette,' in the little village Windsor. As a great number who borrow the paper arc ablo to pay for it, we sin-

AT23. cerely hope they wilCesist from this ncfari ous practice of injuring the Printer by taking the bread out of his mouth. Our paper scarcely reaches the Subscriber's door, before neighbor such a one sends to borrow it Jor a short time, and it is not unfiequently lent round to several more good neighbors before its return to its rightful owner: and when he is lucky enough to get it, he finds it mutilated to such a degree that it cannot be read. It will now be asked, what business is it to the Printer whether people borrow it or not, if the Subscriber has a mind to lend his paper ? We will just take the liberty to explain : þÿ In the first place, it deprives us of that support which printers in general have a right to expect from the public : þÿ In the second place, it is often the means oi making a good Subscriber wilhdraw his name, as he has so in my to borrow his paper he cannot have a chance to read it himself. And when this subscriber is asked for the payment, he sass, I must j ay and give up taking your paper, as 1 cannot afiord to subscribe for my neighbors ; but we ask, why do you lend your papers ? Fie answers I cannot refuse, as 1 have always lived on friendly terms with my neighbors, 1 am obliged therefore to submit to it for the sake of peace ; now if I discontinue taking it 1 shall not be considerded of an ill natured disposi tion, as 1 have not to send a refusal. þÿ Wind, sor, N. TIIE INHUMAN MOTHER. A woman residing at Nascaluccia, whose husband, a laborer, was employed at some distance during the week, and who came home only on Saturday evening, leaving it again on Monday morning, was in the habit during the absence of her husband, of receiving the visits of a young man The female had a child about eight years of age, who Used to inform his father when this person had been in the house, and who had in this manner procured many a sound beating for his mother ; so that in a short time natural affection gave way to a deadly hatred, and she resolved to remove her innocent offspring, whose presence was a continual restraint upon her depraved inclinations.

va strait® asat ®:a©238»2sr<&s atss» One morning the smell of burnt flesh was perceived to proceed from the house, so strong as to be offensive to the neighbours, who enquired the cause of this disagreeable odour. The woman said she had heated her oven, and that the faggots w hich she used for the purpose being kept in an out house had become wet and dirty. As she did not seem in any way disconcerted by their questions, but continued singing to herself, as she appeared busied in her household affairs nothing was suspected. On Saturday, the father came back as usual, and his first enquiry was for the boy ; the wife feigning surprise, asked if he had not gone with him, for so she had believed, not having seen him since Sunday evening, and instantly began to express the most violent grief, beating her breast and tearing her hair, so that even the husband was deceived, and the child was supposed to have wandered and lost itself in the woods. The successful perpetration of one crime led as it usually does, to the perpetration of another. She determined to destroy her husband and marry the young man, whose visits had carried her to the fiendlike extremity of murdering her own child. With the assistance of this person she dispatched the poor man in bed, enveloped his body in a sheet, and buried it in a cavern at a short distance from the v.llage. In a few days the teeiid odour of the corpse attracted the dogs of the neighbourhood to the spot, who tearing and scratching up the earth, laid bare part of the body, winch being discovered enquiries were

put on foot. The husband had not returned, according to custom, for several Saturdays þÿ Sugar from Beet root. þÿ 1'he corpse was examined, but though the features could no longer be traced, the sheet in þÿw hiehit was wrapped, was recognized as belonging to the female : it was also proved that she had given linen and a matrass, both steeped in blood to a washerwoman who revealed the circumstance. The widow and the young man were both arrested and condemned, the latter to be executed; the former whose confession had assisted the conviction of the other to perpetual imprisonment The murder of the child still remained undiscovered. The man, perhaps hoping for a reprieve to the last moment, did not wish to aggravate his case, by confessing his knowledge of a murder still more horrible than that for which he was condemned. But it happened most extraordinry, that after undergoing the sentence of the law, and his body had been consigned to his family for burial, it was perceived that life was not wholly extinct. His friends called in a surgeon whose care finally restored him A circumstance so surprising could no longer be concealed, and before he recovered sufficiently to effect his escape from the neighbourhood, the police became aware of the fact. Reference was made to the judges, and they gave it as their opinion, that having already suffered the final sentence of the Court he was not amenable to its jurisdiction for the same offence.

Fearful of not escaping so well on a second experiment of the gallows, and irritated at having been already carried there by disposition of the woman lie revealed, on a promise of pardon, the murder of the child, in which it did not appear that he had participated þÿ gay suit of scarlet, with the proper The poor boy had been taken from his bed whilst asleep by his unnatural mother, who put him in the oven, and heaping brushwood and faggots over him, set them on fire and closed the oven door ; but the fumes of the burnt flesh escaping, had occasioned the offensive odour which had been remarked by her neighbours. Notwithstanding the perpetration of two crimes so atrocious, the infamous creature, though condemned did not suffer the death appointed by law. There prevailed at the time in Sicily, an invincible repugnance to consign females into the hands of the executioner. .She was removed into one of those horrid dungeons, called daneuse excavated in the rock many feet below the surface of the earth ; low, narrow, and so damp, that the floor is often under water; a lingering and protracted punishment, by which the sufferers perish piecemeal, in a manner far more horrible than by the executioner.

THE ROSE. þÿ The Spirit paus'd, in silent thought ; What grace was there that flower has not ? þÿ Twas but a moment, þÿ þÿo er the Rose A veil of moss the angel throws, And, þÿrob i d n þÿNature simplest s weed, Could there a flower that rose exceed þÿ? Well might the Queen of Flowers be styled the emblem of virtue ; the pride of our gardens attracts all eyes by its modest beauty and unobtrusive elegance ; and while it perfumes the air around it, bends its gentle head before the rude gale, and withers under the scorching rays of the noontide sun; but even in death, when its blushing beauties are scattered in our path þÿ a sad momento of w hat must be the |ot of all earthly loveliness þÿ it retains its odour; so virtue, however humble the path she may traverse, claims the homage of even the wicked. However they may seotf they cannot but respect her ; like the rose, she blooms without ostentation, shunning publicity ; the chilling indifference of the worldly and thoughtless bid her shrink into herself. She bows b fore the storm, but, like the rose, puts forth new blossoms; like the rose, death cannot destroy her sweets; the actions of the virtuous outlive their tomb, and often earn for their memory the praise that was denied to them when living.

A MAN HANGED IN MISTAKE. (From the Waterford Chronicle ) Several doubts have been entertained respecting the identity of the unfortunate man who sobered the extreme penalty of the law upon Saturday week. It is a painful but a no less solemn duty we have now to perform, in stating that facts have come to our knowledge since that time which afford every possible reason tor believing that those doubts are well founded that the name of the prisoner was Edmund Pine, and not Savage þÿ and that so far ironi having murdered his wife, the illfated being was never married. It mav appear astonishing that no witness were brought iorward to support his innocence, but so certain was the prisoner of an acquittal from want of evidence, that he never took a single precaution for his safety until the power of doing so had passed away. In addition to this circumstance, he was constantly subject to failing lits, winch 111 a great degree derang-

ed the faculties of bis mind, and r< ride red him a miserable object. It will be remembered by those present during the trial, that three witnesses who were brought for the prosecution declared themselves unable to identify the prisoner when confronted with him in the dock. The witness who swore to his identity was a brother of the murdered woman, and he observed that there was a mark <e cut upon the cheek of the murderer, and that a similar one was on the chin of the prisoner. Previous to his execution he was shaved, and no sueli mark was found upon him. After his sentence, and until the moment of his execution, he continually and in the most solemn manner declared his innocence ; his riot doing so upon the scaffold was owing to the agitation which, from addressing an immense multitude, might have disturbed bis dying mo riicuts. He It .ft it, however, as a last request upon the Reverend Mr Prendergrast, the clergyman whom we before stated as having attended him with the most unwearied assiduity, to make known bis innocence as far as it was corroborated by the various testimonies that have since come to light. One of the strongest is the following: þÿ The sister of the real murderer, Savage, having obtained permission to visit her brother, proceeded to the condemned cell, but immediately on seeing him turned back again, exclaiming that the man was not her brother, it is said that on being first arrested, be acknowledged bis name to be Savage ; it is, however, right to

mention also that he returned an affirmative to every interrogatory put to him ; in short, the falling sickness we before mentioned had the effect of reducing him to the state of a simpleton or an idiot. No blame can be attached to the jury that found him guiitv ; they pronounced their verdict according to the evidence before them ; but when it is recollected that nine years have elapsed since the commission of the tragic deed, that the greater number of the witnesses were unable to identity him, that Mr Ronayne asserted, if the prisoner was real y the murderer, no man had ever undergone a greater change, and that the story of the prisoner was fully borne out bv a letter which we subjoin from Mr Acheles Wood, of the parish of Kilrnichacl, in the coutity of Cork ; when, we say, that these leading features in the late tragic scene are brought to mind, the doubts of the public will scarcely þÿ founded : be considered unjustifiable or unþÿ I certify that I knew a man hv the name of Edmund Pine, who lived in the parish of Kiliniehael from his infancy, until on or about twenty yea's since he le't his country. He writes now to be in Waterford jail on suspicion of being bv the name of one Savage, who murdered his wife eight years h -nee. 1 knew Edmund Pine and family to be of unexceptionable character whilst in this country. Achf.li.es Wood. þÿ Of Gunancreah, in the parish of Kilmichad and county of Cork. þÿ Dec I, þÿ1831. Savage, or, as we should now call him Edmund Pine, is described as being of the most

industrious and frugal habits. Our readers will remember the extraordinary phenomenon with which this Island was visited in January last, and will no doubt be gratified to learn, that although the ashes which fell here in such abundance originated from a volcanic eruption, that no lives were lost from its effects. The following account, was received here on Saturday, and may be relied upon : þÿ > The sand which was noticed here in January last and supposed to be the effects of the bursting of a volcano, is now accounted for by the following statement from an officer of H. M. S. Gannett, which he learnt at Chagres. The sand issued from an eruption of a volcano in the mountain of Cosiquina, which took place on the morning of the 23d of January last. This account was collected from the Spaniards at Nicaragua. The inhabitants of the village of Masava heard strange reports towards N W., and saw the matter ascending perpendicularly, and descending into a line to the northward against the wind. Some of the sand fell at least 300 miles from the volcano ! The same sand shower was experienced at Segovia at the same time, accompanied with slight shocks of an earthquake. At Grenada, Nicaragua, about 75 miles from it, the explosion was so dreadful, that at one þÿo clock in the morning when it commenced, every thing was involved in pitchy darkness ; Men, women, and children, took shelter in the Churches ; and the wild beasts from the forests sought the protection of man, by entering their

houses, and the birds of the air of all descriptions were flying through the streets in extreme alarm, until 3 þÿo clock, p. m. when the daikness terminated ; and I am happy to add, says the narrator, that awful as was the þÿex plosion no lives were lost. Several estates, and much cattle were destroyed near the Mount. þÿ St. Lucia May 27.

A most singular event has occurred in the family of a noble lord, which, however unpleasant to the teelings of the parties concerned, it will be impossible long to keep from the knowledge of the public. We have, therefore, no scruple in stating what wrc have heard respecting it Lady B. having lost some jewels last week, in the same mysterious way in which other robberies of a similar kind have been committed, sent for two police-officers to institute a rigorous inquiry amongst the domestics of the establishment. The only individual whom her Ladyship proposed to exempt from personal search was her own maid ; of whose integrity and excellent qualities although she had been with her but a few months, Lady B. entertained so high an opinion that she could not bear the idea of treating her as an object of suspicion The officers arrived ; and after a very short visit, came at once to the astonished Lady B. and told her, Madam, not only must your maid be searched, but she is the only person here who need'- be searched ; for the maid has got your jewels ; and, what is more þÿ the maid is a man ! The fact was soon proved to the satisfaction of all beholders. The maid was a returned convict þÿ a young man sentenced to transportation for life for various ingenious robberies, but who had made his escape, and assumed female apparel as the best mode of returning to this country with impunity. Of his extraordinary dexterity no better proof can be given titan the fact, that for eight months he had lived in
Lady þÿB. s family without the slightest suspicion being entertained as to Ins sex, and had

®A.W8!R TOSTCRBISX won the confidence of his mistress by the uniform propriety of his conduct. The affair is a very awkware one, and we really do not know' what precautions ladies must take in future when forced to change their personal attendants. We pity lady B. most sincerely for the very painful situation in which she has been placed, and wish that it were possible to guard effectually against similar impositions. þÿ liertjord Reformer.

Fame. þÿ After all that is said of fame þÿ who has it? Baron Munchansen, Robinson Crusoe, and Mother Hubbard Noble rivalry! to enter the field against the latter lady and her dog. Fame ! þÿ who gives it ? a snarling, snappish, currish critic from his chimney-corner. Who greedily thieves and pilfers it all ? old, weak, bald-headed Time. CONSUMPTION. A young lady in the last stages of consumption, was lately restored to health by the following extraordinary and accidental remedy: þÿ She had long been attended by the faculty, but derived no benefit from their prescriptions, and considered herself verging to the end of her existence, when she retired during the summer to a vale in the country, with the intention to wait in solitude the hour of her approaching dissolution. While in that situation, it was her custom to rise as early as her malady would permit, and contemplate the beauties of nature and the wonderful works of God from her chamber window, from which she observed a dog belonging to the house, with scarcely any flesh on bis bones, constantly go and lick the dew off a camomile bed in the garden; in doing which the animal was noticed to alter in appearance, to recover strength, and finally to look plump and well. The singularity of the circumstance was impressed Strongly on the þÿlady mind, s and induced her to try what effect might be produced lroni following the þÿdog example. s She accordingly procured the dew from the same bed ol camomile, drank a small quantity each morning, and, after continuing it some time, experienced some relief ; her appetite became regular, and she found a return of spirits, and in the end was completely cured. þÿ Caledonian Mercury.

Table salt is a mineral with which all are familiarly acquainted ; but a knowledge of that spoken of in the New Testament may throw light upon the text in which our þÿLord disci- s ples are compared to the salt of the earth ; which, if it loose its savour, is cast out and trodden under foot The salt alluded to was probably fossil salt, which, containing, as such salt generally does, a large portion of ochrey clay or eartv matter, was liable from exposure to become insipid. Accordingly, Maudrell, in his journey to Jerusalem, tells us that in the Valley of Salt on the side towards Gibal, from a small precipice formed by the continual taking away of the salt, he broke a piece of which the part that had been exposed to the sun. rain, and air, though it contained sparks and particles of salt, had entirely lost its savor þÿSire, as he found part while that its next the rocks still retained saltness Salt which had thus become insipid might be used for the purpose of repairing roads ; or ca t out to / e trodden under foot þÿ Moore's Ancient Mineralogy.

We perceive by the Courier de la Martinique, that a treaty has been entered into at Copenhagen between the government of England, France and Denmark, for the suppression of the slave trade. Vessels under the Danish flag, which may be detained by English or French cruizers employed on the coast of America, are to be given over to the Danish authorities at St. Croix. Those taken on the African station are to be carried into Christianburg on the Cold Coast of Guinea, and those taken on the Madagascar station, wiil be taken to either of the above Danish possessions, O'- 1 > Tranquebar in the East Indies, should circumstances rendei this last destination the most convenient. This treaty was ratified by the King of the French on the 2d of December last. I wo 1' rench vessels of war had sailed for Para for the protection of the French inhabitants and property in that city.

The suspicions which we expressed the other day touching the reality of an announced þÿg eat reduction of military establishments in the Continental States, have not been removed bv the accounts received since through the Foreign Papers. Accounts from the Hague, under the date of February 4, state that letters from Frankfort confirm a report which had previously existed ot an intended augmentation of the garrison of Luxembourg by troops of the Gei manic Confederation. It is now admitted that the garrison of that fortress is to lie put on the same footing as at the time of the hostilities between Holland and Belgium þÿ which means that the garrison is to be reinforced, in this time of þÿ profound peace," to the full arnouut of a complete war establishment. Does tins look like a speedy concession of the claims of Belgium, and a consequent settlement of the dispute with Holland ? Whatever may be done, we hope the Duke of Wellington will not imitate the late dandy Secretary for Foreign Allairs by adding either an appendix to the absurd Anglo iallicau Convention, or a new volume to the protocols If a word of advice be thrown away upon the hostile parties, and further than one word ot advice our Government ought not to go þÿ let us hear no more of London Conferences, or protocols, or þÿ peaceful þÿwars, or þÿ amicable þÿembargoes, or þÿ demonstraþÿtions, that demonstrate nothing except the folly of making them; but let Belgium and H nihind be permitted fairly to light their

qu :rrel out. If Belgium, with double the population, is unable to meet Holland single handed, she is neither lit for, nor entitled to, independence. She must either be a French or a Dutch piovince, and it is for the interest ol Lngland that Belgium should not belong to I ranee. The new contingent to the garrison of Luxembourg is to be furnished by the States of Wirtcrnburg, Baden, Hesse Hohen zollern, Hesse Homburg, and Frankfort We are disposed to believe that the announced disarmament by Austria is a mere pretence. Some petty reductions are of no consequence, while she keeps up her immense armies in Italy, and the Tyrol bristles with bayonets. It is not at the time when Russia pours fresh battalions into Poland þÿ when the petty German States are called upon to furnish their contingents, to place the garrison of Luxembourg upon the war establishment þÿ

and when the independence of Switzerland is once more threatened by its ancient enemy, that Austria will think proper to throw oil' her burnished panoply, lay aside her spear, and bind her brows so long cased in steel wilh the olive branch. No þÿ though we are now in the twentieth year of þÿ general þÿpeace, the time has not yet arrived when their restless ambition will permit to Sovereigns of Europe to convert the sword into the plough-share, and the speat into the pruning hook, and to allow the people to follow the arts of peaceful industrv, without being disturbed by the movements of armies or the alarms of war. þÿ Morning He rani, February 13.

DANDRl£U. » - j <>-"- Whilst Admiral de Ruyter, in his expedition of 1033, was at anchor near the Castle of St. George, on the coast of Guinea, th>ee of his sailors who were ashore went into a house where ardent spirits were sold, and, getting drunk, extinguished the lights, and began to Jiyht witb their knives 'I he Landlord, who came in to separate the.rn, received a wound of which he died; and there was no possibility of discovering the murderer, as all three denied it alike positively. General Valkenburg, the governor of the forts and magazines in Africa which belonged to the Dutch West India Company, warned the whole three to prepare for death, adding, that lots should be cast to determine which of them should be executed. He upon whom the lot fell was hanged. When it was thought he was dead, the rope was cut, and. preparations were making for his burial, when signs of life, were perceived. Means were used fir his recovery, which proved success ful ; and a message was sent to Valkenbury to inquire what was to be done with him. The general answered that he must die, according to the tenor of his sentence ; but De Ruyter was of a different opinion, alleging it was by no means certain that this unfortunate man was the perpe.rafor of the crime, as the lot might fall upon the in-

nocent as readily as upon the guilty ; that since it had pleused God to preserve his life as it were by a miracle, it would be wrong to deprive him of it ; besides, that the punishment he had already suffered was sufficient to expiate, the crime, and to serve as an example. Yalkenburg yielded tn these reasons, and the sailor urns spared. He was afterwards interrogated Concerning the state of his feelings during the inflEtion of punishment, and declared he remembered almost nothing that had Happened that day, having, after sentence was pronounced, lost all powers of recollection ; except thct, when he was thrown off the ladder, it seemed to hire thai he was falling into a deep well.

(Barbados Bridge-town , March 28, 1835.) VV e rejoice, that by the blessing of God, a beginning is at last made in the rebuilding of our Parish Churches. The following description of the laying the first stone of St. John's Church has been kindly communicated to us. We hope soon to have the pleasure of publishing intelligence of the same interesting character from the other parishes which still remain without their Churches. On Thursday the 26th instant the Foundation Stone of the Church about to be re erected in the Parish of Saint John, was laid. A large number of ladies and gentlemen from that and the neigbouring Parishes were assembled to witness the ceremony. The procession moved from the liectory-house at 12 o'clock, in the following order : þÿ Children o f Parochial and other Schools Members of the Friendly Societies Gentlemen of the Vestry Students of Codrington College Other Gentlemen of the Parish and neighbourhood Clergy of the Island THE MODEL OF CHURCH, in cedar, carried by the Architect The Archdeacon of Barbados Edmund Haynes, Esq., by whom the Stone was to he laid. On arriving at the proposed site of the new Church, the gentlemen occupied the ground on each side of the Archdeacon, the ladies being in front under an awning raised for the occasion An appropriate Prayer, followed by the Lord's Prayer, was then read by the Ai' hdcaron : after which, a silver trowel was

x>AB3£ vastmroasK mstmwaiTQS ATIS. delivered by the Honorable J. II. Nurse to Edmund Haynes, Esq., who laid the stone in the usual form. This part of the ceremony having been concluded, the Children of the Schools, joined by some of the Clergy and Laity, sung the 100th Psalm ; after which, the Archdeacon pronounced the Blessing and the procession moved back to the Rectory -house in the same order.

A private in the militia killed in resisting the Marshal in the execution of his duty. An unfortunate occurrence took place, a few days ago, in the Parish of St. Tl oriias in the Vale, which led to the loss of file. The circumstances, as they have been detailed to us, arc as tbllows: A Rlr Simon Pcacan, who, resides at the above rocks, bad for the last eight years evaded the authority vested in the hands of the Colonel of the Regiment,; by resisting every attempt to compel him to do militia duty. The consequence was, that the other militia men residing in the same district, were very negligent in their attendance at parade ; and on an enquiry being instituted into the cause, it was stated, that if Mr. l'eacari could resist the Colonel's authority, others were determined to avail themselves of his example. A Court- Martial was ordered to assemble for the trial of Private Pcacan, and him, was wholly disregarded. The upon a notice, which was regularly served trial, however, took place, and he was sentenced to pay a fine of £50, or he confined in the common gaol for 28 days. Of the result of the trial, due notice was given to him by the Marshal of the Regiment, who was resisted in taking the delinquent into custody. The commanding officer, on finding his authority thus and two men lo aid the completely set at defiance, ordered a corporal Regimental Marshal in the execution of his duty. They proceeded to the habitation of Mr.'Peacan, who, after using very violent and abusive language, sur-
rendered himself, and invited the party into

the house, where a guard was placed over him, in consequence of his refusal to comply with the terms of the Court-Martial. The Marshal was sent to procure further aid to remove the prisoner ; but, shortly after the Marshal's departure, their prisoner became very outrageous ; made a rusli from his room ; knocked down the sentinel who was guarding him, and made an effort to secure a doublebarrelled gun hanging up in the hall. One of the militia men, in his attempt to prevent him from obtaining possession of the gun, was knocked down, and very much maltreated ; and, on calling to his comrade to protect bis life, the latter, after three distinct warnings to Peacan, discharged Lis pistol at him ; but not appearing to have taken effect, he discharged his second pistol, which put an end to the conflict. A oroner's Inquest sat upon the vestigation, returned a verdict þÿ body of Mr Peacan, and after a " putient in- That the deceased came to his death bv pistol balls discharged by a Private of the Militia in defence of his life, and in the execution of his duty." þÿ Jamaica Despatch, Feb. 25.

Awful Visitation of Providence. þÿ On Friday night, a woman named Price, the wife of a soldier in the Coldstream Guards residing in Orchard-street, Westminster, having got into a dispute with a neighbour while both were in a state of intoxication, suddenly dropptd down dead, while imprecating the vengeance of the Almighty, and making use of the words, " I wish God may strike me dead if " .She said no more. Assistance was procured, but the vital spark had fled. She was only 35 years of age, of a very quarrelsome disposition, and very much addicted to drinking. þÿ Sundry Times.

There are two or three monkies in the Zoological gardens in the Regent's park whose passion for snuff affords much amusement to the visitors. They seem to rub it zealously into their eyes and ears, as well as their nostrils, and, after some minutes of triumphant sneezing and snorting, to enjoy the narcotic influence of the Nicotian weed with the calm contentment of an old fashioned philosopher. Fashion makes people visit when they would rather stay at home, eat when they are not. hungry, and drink when they arc not thirsty.

The written accounts from various parts of the Continent represent the winter as having set in with extreme harshness This is the severest winter known at Naples within the last fifteen years. There was ice on the streets of the city, a most rare occurrence, on Christmas-dav and the two proceeding davs, and all the surrounding mountains have been covered with snow for the last ten dav s. I n Calabria seven dealers in lish were overwhelmed by the snow They were returning to Naples with several carts of fresh water fish on the 23d of December, and when passing by a place called Stranda di Cinque .VI iglia, the snow fell upon them from the impending height and buried the unfortunate men, with their carts, horses, Arc. It is estimated that it will require a hundred men for eight days to remove the snow and disengage the bodies.

The fate of Genies. þÿ Some one has desired me to describe the influence which men of genius have in this land: that can be done in a word they have none. The editors of two or three leading newspapers have more to say with the country and with the government than all the bards who have breathed for these fifty years. The influence of genius is recorded in its fortunes. Chatterton drank poison, for he could not find bread ; Johnson was refused the means of improving his health abroad ; Burns, at his death, had neither bread in his house nor a penny in his pocket ; Crabbe died a poor person þÿ preferment did not find him out; Scott crushed himself in attempting independence, and his country refuses to save his books from the auctioneer ; Byron was exiled, and du d almost cursing the land his genius adorns ; Coleridge has been deprived of his small pension; Wordsworth lives by distributing stamps ; Southey has a pint of thin w ine a day from the king ; Moore has found verse, like virtue, its own reward. Hogg picks a mutton bone on Yarrow ; and Wilson lives on moral philosophy. þÿ Cunningham.

The Goddess of Reason, þÿ In the Paris papers of August 1. 1817, we find among the obituaries the following announcement: þÿ "Died, within these few days, in the hospital for pauper lunatics of Saltpetriere, where site had lived unpitiedandunknownformany years, the famous Theroinge de Mericourt (the God dess of Reason), the most remarkable of the heroines oi' the Revolution." This temale (nearly in a state of nudity) was seated upon a throne by Fouche and Carnot, in die Champ de Mars, and hailed alternately as the Goddess of Reason and of Liberty There was something remarkable in the history of the latter days of this poor creatuie, and her life is not without its moral. She, who was taught publichly to blaspheme her Creator, and to dishonour her sex (for she appeared in public near! naked), was for the last twenty years of la r miserable life, subject to the greatest of human calamities þÿ the deprivation of reason. She repented severely of her hot rible crimes, and her few lucid intervals were tilled up by the most heart-rending lamentations She died at the age of fifty-seven. This is another awful warning to the living Atheists, Radicals, and " Free thinking Christians," who are now following to the steps ot'the French Revolutionists.

Two Turkish officers of high rank have arrived in London, and were presented to the Duke of Wellington The sole object of their journey is to see and become acquainted with England. They are from the interior of the Seraglio, and hold rank in the Imperial Guard. One of them, Azmi Bey, is son of the late Minister of Foreign Affairs ; and they have been instructed by the Sultan to Mr. Urquhart. þÿ The Duke of Wellington, who received them with great courtesy, regretted, at their interview with him, they had visited London at so dreary and dark a season of the year. < )ne of them answered, " Since we have boon in England we have been daily seeing new lights, -and have no reason to complain of the darkness of your atmosphere."

A curious discovery has been recentlv made 11 a Swedish copper-mine. On opening a gallery between two levels, some miners (bun t the bodyofavoung man in a spot 150 feet deep, which had not been visited in the memory of man. The weak solution of sulphuric acid in water, with the alkalies which had formed there, had petrified the corpse without at all robbing it of its youthful appearance. þÿ So unusual a sight collected the whole neighbourhood together. An old woman soon came up, and bursting into tears upon recognizing the features of her bethrothed bride-groom who had disappeared about this 50 years, but what had become of him never was known. þÿ The interval that had elapsed had wrinkled and furrowed the old dame's lace, whilst the bridegroom, thus disentombed from his grave, appeared in all the fresh lineament of youth. The body was exposed for several days, and lastly interred with much ceremony, being accompanied by the whole body of miners. þÿ London Paper.

HIGHLAND CRITICISM. A Highland Schoolmaster was lately expatiating on the superiority of the language of the Highlands over that of every other country, and, by a natural disgression, came to remark on the inaccuracies, as he conceived them to be, of the English tongue. In order to prove his many and grievous charges against propriety he selected the word Hypocrite, by way of illustration. " Here," said lie, in the broad accent of Mull, "you call a man that's faithless to his religious profession, a Heepocreet, and a woman of the same character, you call her a Heepocreet ; now," said the learned Doland, rearing back his head with an air of dignity that might have done or the great Lexiographer himself, " if the 'man be a Heepocreet, both common sense and the gender of the noun must tell you, that the woman ought to be called a Sheep þÿocreet.- Kilmarnock Journal.

An anecdote, which we believe mav be depended upon as authentic, was lately current at Madrid, which exhibits the inefficiency of commercial prohibitions. Foreign paper is a contraband article in Spain, and yet it is pretty regularly imported from England. Thelady of the Cabinet Minister iiau formerly visited Madrid, and being particularly pleased with the writing paper which she purchased there, imagined there was none other in the world so good þÿ none other upon which it w as possible to write. Upon her return to the neighbourhood London, she made arrange- of ments for receiving regular and periodical supplies of her favourite papei from Madrid. It happened, however, in the course of time, that she was disappointed of her usual package, and after her patience was exhausted by writing, she wrote to the British Minister at Madrid, and requested him to call upon the dilatory, paper man. Mr. Addington did so, and what was the answer ?" ALARM IN d INUNDATION IN INDIA. From the Calcutta Courier of Aug. 1(5.)

Accounts arc corning in of a very extensive inundation produced by the freshes of the Damooda, which is reported to have broken its banks and laid the whole country under water between Chinsurah and Burdwan. þÿ We hear that some lives have been lost hy the torrents sweeping away native huts in the

Ancient Maidens and Widows. þÿ Mr. Hayley in his very ingenious and pleasant þÿ Essay on Old þÿMaids, gives the argument of one of the debaters upon the foliowing question þÿ þÿ Which is the most eligible for a wife, a widow or an old maid þÿ! þÿ The oratorinsisted, that a man who married an old maid had a greater chance of being beloved by his wife than he who wedded a widow The affection of a remarried widow, he maintained, was a pocket telescope, which she directed towards her good man in the grave, and it enlarged to a monstrous degree all the mental and personal endowments of the dear departed. j not in a vault of brick or stone. She then turned the inverted glass to his diminishing successor, and, whatever his proportion ol excellence might be the poor, luckless, living mortal soon dwindled in her sight it a comparative pigmy. But this was not the ease with the old maid. No; her allection was a portable microscope, which magnified in a stupendons mannei all the attractive merits of her spouse þÿ he filled her mind, occupied her eye, engrossed her heart. I he widow (the orator admitted) was generally preferred to the old maid ; but the

to wan lor the favourable minute, and struck in ilie very instant when the fish bad fairly risen to the book ; while the old maid was an angler whom fruitless expectation bad rendered impatient þÿ she was thrown into tiepidation by the appearance ol the nibble , and by making a too hasty movement, she often rendered her bait an object ol alarm. He compared a weeping widow to the moaning by ana þÿ that artlul, destructive, and insatiable creature winch lured into its den by a treacherous cry ol distress the unwary traveller whom it intended to devour. Chaucer, he said made Ins Wife ot Bath glory in having buried lour husbands, and express a perfect readiness, whenever Heaven might give her the opportunity, to engage with a fifth þÿ! and Chaucer, he insisted, copied nature most faithfully. þÿ Now the old maid, good soul ! remembering how long she had waited for her first husband, instead ot hastily looking forward toa second, direetcu all her attention to cherish and preserve the dear creature whom she had at last acquired. He had no rival to fear either among the living or the dead. þÿ It was of liilnnie importune! , lie maintained, to matrimonial felicity, that the husband should receive into Ins arms a partner lor hie, whose disposition and habits, instead ol being fixed by a loi liter lord, were to be moulded according to the will and abilities ol her first and only In tins point, the widow was a petce ol warped wood, winch the most skilful workman might lind himself unable to shape

as lie wished þÿ hut the old maid was the pliant virgin wax, which lollows with the most happy ductility every serious design, every ingenious device, every sportive whim of the modeller. In conclusion the speaker conjured every gentleman, who might happen to hesitate between a widow and an old maid, to remember that reason and experience, that equity and the general interest of mankind, all loudly pleaded for his preferring the latter. He entreated him to recollect, that the man who married a widow had great cause to apprehend unreasonable expectations, unpleasant comparisons and variable allection þÿ while he who married and old maid might with conlidence prepare to meet unexacting tenderness, increasing tenderness, and perpetual endearments.

LOWER CANADA. We have received New Brunswick papers to the 28th of April. From these we learn the situation of the contending parties in Lower Canada, (to which we have before alluded), and wliieh will be best communicated to our leaders by the following extract : þÿ two and three þÿo clock, time when most of Qucbec, March 18. þÿ The session ol the Provincial Parliament was closed this day at two þÿo clock. The þÿFelon Counsel s Bill, the onlv one passed by both Houses, was reserved for the royal sanction. The following is a copy of Lord þÿAylmer sspeech on the occasion : þÿ þÿ Gentlemenof the Legislative Council, þÿ Gentlemenof the House of Assembly, þÿ It appears bv the customary official reports transmitted to me daily by the Jit ik of the House of Assembly, that for some days past the attendance of a sufficient number of members to constitute a quorum has been wanting, to enable the Assembly to proceed to business; and as it may be inferred from some recent proceedings of tlte Assembly that no further business will be transacted in that branch of the Provincial Parliament, I can no longer feel justified, notwithstanding mv great anxiety, to prolong the present session, in detaining from their homes and usual occupations, those members of the two Houses of the Provincial Parliament who may he disposed to persevere in the perlbrrnauce of their legislative daties. þÿ Gentlemen of the House of Assembly, þÿ 1 have upon this occasion only to express my regret, that the present session should

have failed in producing those measures of relief, in relation to the financial difficulties of the province, which are so urgently required under existing circumstances. þÿ It would have afforded me much gratification, had I been able to report to H is Maþÿjesty s Government that the responsibility so generously incurred, with the view of relieving in some measure the urgent wants of the public service, had ceased to exist, by the re payment, from out of the public funds of the province, of the advance equal thirty-one to thousand pounds sterling, made in pursuance of the instructions of the late Secretary of State for the Colonial Department, from the military chest. þÿ þÿ entlemen of the // ouse of Assembly, - Gentlemen of the Legislative Council, þÿ I informed you at the opening of the : þÿ present session that I was then in possession of important communications, and that l expected to receive others from //is Government, upon subjects of vital importance to the interests of the province. The communications which were adverted to on that occasion, as having been received, have been since laid before you, but 1 have not yet received those which I then informed you i expected to receive, and which 1 have every reason to believe must now lie ncai at hand. That the expected despatches will possess an extraordinary degree of importance to the general interests of the prov ince, and w ill

require that communications should take place, in relations to their contents, between the head of the Executive Government and the two // ouses of t ho Provincial Parliament, can hardly admit of a doubt being entertained, when it is considered that the Committee of the J/ouse of Commons to whom were referred, in the last session of the Imperial Parliament, on certain matters relating to the affairs of this province, including the petition of the 11 ouse of Assembly, dated 1st of March, 1834, recommended, with reference to the unhappy differences existing between the two branches of the Colonial Legislature, as well as between the J/ouse of Assembly and li is þÿMajesty s Government, that the practical measures for the future administration of Lower Canada, should be left to the mature consideration of the Government responsible for their adoption and execution þÿ Under these circumstances, the premature termination of the session, which is now unavoidable, is an event deeply to he þÿregretted.

AWFUL CALAMITY. The whole of New Orleans, lias been thrown into consternation by a calamity which is thus put forth in the Louisiana Advertiser. On Friday morning, between the hours of (a our citizens are reposing from their labors, and, perhaps, not even dreaming of the dreadful calamities of their fellow creatures) that large and extensive building in þÿ( anal-street, known as the Planter's Hotel, fell to the ground with a tremendous crash, and gave a shock to the surrounding neighbourhood, similar to that experienced from an earthquake ; þÿ an awful pause ensued for a few seconds, when the smothered voices of several unfortunate individuals who were deeply buried beneath the ruins issued from the pile; tho alarm hells rang and hundreds of onr efficient firemen rushed upon the spot, and made every exertion humanity could dictate to rescue the the miserable sufferers from the jaws of death. We understand that they were from CO to 70 persons living in the house, some of whom succeeded in effecting their escape, with but little or no injury, but we are sorry to add that several have lost their lives or been miserably mutilated. It is tiis mercy that there have not been many more victims in the list, as the billardrooms had been remarkably full, and several persons whom we have seen had scarcely quitted them when they heard the crash. As usual, on such awful opportunities, there were some demons in the shape of human beings, who repaired therefor the sake of plunder ; we arc glad to hear, for the honor of our city,

that some of them have been taken and imprisoned in the gaol. During the three days revolution in Paris, some persons, who were similarly industrious, were instantly seized, and the populace punished them with summary justice; we almost regret not to have a paraded to relate, for if summary justice is ever justifiable, there never was a strongei necessity for it than on the present occasion. Various reports are in circulation as to the number of persons who were within the walls when they gave way : but it is supposed þÿMajesty s there were not less than sixty. What became of the whole of them, can only be surmised ; many, it is said, miraculously escaped at the instant, while otic shudders to think of w hat the ruins may yet conceal from the view. þÿ United States Gazette.

MELANCHOLY SUICIDE OF REAR- ADMIRAL LEWIS. ( From the Morning Herald, May S.) An inquisition was yesterday afternoon taken at No 2, Avenue-road, þÿRegent park, sbefore Mr. Stirling, on view of the body of Rear-Admiral Joint Lewis, aged t»5, who on Wednesday morning terminated his existence by blowing out Lis brains with a pistol, at his residence as above. þÿ Mr. Francis Edward Hicks, surgeon, of 83, George-sireet, l.anover square, was the first witness called, and said that he had attended the deceased and his family professionally for the last nine months. About six weeks since tie was called in tiie middle of the night to attend one of the daughters of the deceased, when lie had a Iona conversation with the Admiral, in the course of which lie observed lor the first time that, he was evidently labouring under strong mental affliction. Witness saw him again on the Monday preceding his death, when he appeared extremely melancholy and desponding. About seven þÿo clock on the Wednesday alluded to he was sent for in haste to the residence of the deceased ; and on his arrival he found the unfortunate gentleman lying on the bed in his sleeping- room, quite dead, and covered witii blood On examination he found that a ball had entered the light temple, passing out on the opposite side, lacerating in its progress the anterior lobe of the brain, which must have caused almost instant death. There were two pocket pistols Ling on the lloor, one of which had recently been discharged ; and on examining the wmdowshutter he ob-

served a mark, as if made by a pistol bullet ; the ball, however, was no where to be found. þÿ Lieutenant John Lewis, in the lion. East India þÿCompany Madras s service, and son of the deceased, was next called. IJe stated that lie lived in the same house with his father, and had many opportunities of observing his conduct. He had latterly conducted himself in a very strange manner. He conversed with him the night previous to his death, and his language was then very incoherent. He slept by himself, and retired to his chamber about eight þÿo clock. About seven the next morning he was alarmed by the report of a pistol coming from the þÿdeceased sbed-room. Witness instantly repaired thither, and found his father extended on the floor. There was a dreadful wound in his temple, evidently inflicted by a pistol shot. Two pistols were lying on the floor. With assistance he lifted him on the bed, where he expired in about a quarter of an hour. þÿ Juror : Was your father married? Witness: He was, 1 believe, recently married, after having been a widower 20 years. þÿ Did his wife reside in the house ? She did not. þÿ Did you ever have any words witii him on the subject of tiffs marriage? Un the event coming to my knowledge for the first time on Tuesday night, 1 certainly remonstrated witii him on the impropriety of the match, but we had no violent quarrel, and I told him as lie had done wrong, we must make the best of it. Was not his wife here on the previous day ? I believe she was, but
I did not see her. þÿ Mrs Rebecca Rotty, the sister of the þÿAdmiral first s wife, was examin-

ed at some length. It appeared from hef statement that the þÿdeceased s present wife was formerly a servant in his establishment, and that he had married her on the Kith of January last. She left directly afterwards; but llie circumstance of the marriage was not known to his family until the day preceding the fatal event. þÿ The Coroner having summed up, the Jury returned a verdict of þÿ Temporary þÿInsanity.

The electric fluid darted through the atmostphere in vivid flashes, with scarcely any intermission, for above a half hour, followed successively by and immediate explosion, the most startling and terrific þÿ the rain pouring in torrents for some time previous to and during this þÿ warning of the þÿelements. For 3 or 4 days preceding the weather had been exceedingly hazy and dense, with occasional heavy showers and light winds Since the storm, there has been a succession of rains, but no bad weather. A Good Shot. þÿ The name of Captain Ross has been so often before the public in various pigeon-shooting matches, that nothing is wanted to establish him as a firstrate shot. I saw him hit a black wafer fixed on the back of a common card at fourteen yards several times ; but, strange to say, he only missed the card twice at this distance out of three hundred shots hitting the water one hundred and fifty-five times. Calling on Captain Ross one morning, I found him practising at fourteen yards. He then presented his pistol out of the drawing-room w indow and said, þÿ Now you shall see me take the head off the figure on Smith þÿBarry s þÿhouse. Tiffs was a small gilt figure of Hope, about five inches in length, placed bewcen the windows, to show that the house was insured at the Hope Insurance office. He lodged the hall in tiie left breast. þÿ That will not þÿdo, said lie 1 must have the head off þÿ Is it not þÿdangerous? said I, þÿ there is S Barry and friend sitting þÿclose. þÿ Oh, no!, replied he, þÿ have I perfect confidence in my þÿpistol. He fired again, and shot off the head ! The distance across the street was certainly not less than fifteen yards ; but the space from Madam Hope to the chairs on, which Smith Barry and his friend were sitting did not exceed tiiree They showed no symptoms of alarm on ascertaining, as they arose to the window, w hence the shot proceeded ; but, on the contrary, they took their seats again quietly after the first fire. Perhaps the following may be termed a chef

Of late years silk-worms have been introduced at Caoe Town; and it is expected that the production of silk in so favourable a climate will all' n d a valuable source o! employment, and, in time, supply the place ol the cultivation of the vine, which has lor several years, as I have already observed, been in a declining state. The scarcity of labour in the interior of the colony will, however, lor a long period, prevent the colonists from availing themselves of this branch of industry; for the management of silk-worms requires both much manual labour and a minute attt ntion, which the farmers ot the imeiior cannot well spare from their other occupations. The management of the milch cows is somewhat pecuhai in this country. The cattic are a mixed breed, between the original African race and the European ; and few ot the eows will give their miik without allowing their calves to suck for some time. But as all the calves are reared to increase the stock, no inconvenience is felt from this circumstance. An oblong enclosure is made with strong poles fixed in the ground, with a pen at one end toconline die calves until tlicy are wanted. Into this pen the calves arc driven before the cows conic home from grazing in the evening. I no cuttle being O <-a never lionscd, become excessively wild; and to catch and tie a young cow to her post in the " kraal," is a matter of iu> small diliicully, and sometimes not tree hum danger, On die first at-
tempt to take hold ol the calf in the held, tlio enraged cow genci.dly runs furiously at the person who presumes to interfere in her family cuuceiiio, w uen he must lake care to yet

But the worst part of his task still remains to be þÿachieved to secure the cow ; and this is as much as two or three people generally can manage 'i be moment the animal perceives that an attempt is made to convey a noose round her horns by means of a long stick, and the attempt fails, she becomes so impatient and shy that it is necessary change to the point of attack. One ol the people now endeavours, by means of the suck, to get the noose round her hind leg when she lifts her loot from the ground, which ojieration requires much dexterity As soon as this end is effected, the thong used for the purpose is drawn tight by assistants, the and secured round one of the poles of the "kraal,'' when the animal becomes perfectly furious, bellowing, kicking, and plunging. Wo be to him that comes within the length of her tether ! for, with inflamed eyes and tongue lolled out, she runs indiscriminately at every tiling that comes within her reach. But, taking advantage of her turnings, the people, who are secure from her rage behind the poles of the ' kraal,' gradually tighten the thong and eonfine her elliirts until her leg is drawn up close to the pole, and they can venture to approach her head and fasten to her horns another thong, which is then conveyed round a pole on the opposite side of the 'kraal.' One thong is then slackened and the other tightened until the cow's head is secured to her post, where she is allowed to fume and bellow till

she is tired and becomes more manageable þÿ At the time of milking, a boy stands at the door ot the pen, and lets the calves out as they are wanted, for they soon learn to answer to their names. After allowing the calf to suck for a few minutes, they proceed to milk all they can get from the cow, which generally retains enough for her young. The quantity of milk the cows yield is in this part of the colony very inconsiderable. Twenty cows seldom give more than from twenty-four to thirty-six quarts at a milking; hut it is genclully very rich in quality It is remarkable, notwithstanding the intractability of the other cattle, that the bulls have none of the ferocity of those in England. þÿ Moodie.

organic and animal life compared. The functions of the organic life are performed with uniiiterupted continuity ; to those of the animal life rest is indispensable. The action of the heart is unceasing; it takes not and needs not rest. On it goes for the space of eighty or ninety years, at the rate of one hundred thousand strokes every twenty-four hours having at every stroke a gre it resistance to overcome, yet continues this action for this length of time without intermission. þÿ Alike incessant is the action <>f the lung, which is always receiving and always emitting air ; and the action of the skit., which is always transpiring and always absorbing ; and the action of the alimentary canal, which is always compensating the loss which the system is always sustaining. But of this continuity of action, the organs and functions of the animal life are incapable. No voluntary muscle can maintain Us action beyond a given time ;

no effort of the will can keep it in a state of unintc.rupted contraction; relaxation must alterriHt" with contraction ; and <ven this alternate action cannot go on long without rest. þÿ No org ui of sense can continue to receive which lie may forthwith proceed to deposit in j impression wilhoul fatigue. By protracted exertion, the ear loses its sensibility to sound, the eve to light, the tongue to savor, and the touch to the qualities of bodies about which it is conversant. The brain cannot carry on its intellectual operations with vigour beyond a certain period ; the trains of ideas with which it works, become, after a time, ind -tinct and confused ; nor is it capable of re-acting with cnergv until it has remained in a state of rest proportioned to the duration of its preceding activity. And this rest is sleep Sleep is the repose of the senses, the rest of the muscles their support and sustenance. What food is to the organic, sleep is to the animal life. þÿ Nutrition can no more go on without aliment than sensation thought and motion, without sleep. þÿ l)r. Southwand Smith.

ABSORBING POWERS OF THE SKIN. Many facts testify the action of absorption by the skin. There are direct experiments to prove that the human hand is capable of imbibing. in a quarter of an hour, an ounce and a half of warm water, that is, that the w hole body is enabled of imbibing, in an hour, six or seven pounds. An interesting narrative is on record, of a ship's crew w ho were exposed at sea for several days in an open boat; thev bad consumed all their water ; they had no fluid of any kind which they could drink ; thev soon began to suffer from thirst ; their feeling at length became intolerable, and the drinking of sea water only increased its intensity. When nearly exhausted, they were exposed, during several hours, to a heavy shower of rain. As soon as their clothes became thoroughly wet their thirst began to abate, and, before the rain had ceased, their thirst was gone. They did not fail to profit by this experience. From this time each man, as lie began to feel thirsty, dipped his shirt in the sea water and wore it next his skin, which had invariably the eflect of removing his thirst, the skin taking in the particles of water, but rejecting the salt diss solved in it. þÿ Denny Cyclopedia. þÿ The late Professor Robinson, of Edinburgh, once bribed a man to let himself grow so thirsty as not to collect a single drop of saliva, and, when the man was in this state, wrapped round Ids throat a cloth soaked in wafer. In a quarter of an hour the man's saliva began to flow freely. It is also said, that the people living on

the shores of the Black Sea, being vorv ill off for want of fresh water, immergc their bodies in the salt springs abounding in these parts, and thus satisly their thirst. \\ e are more particularly anxious to lay these facts before our readers, as there is no saying how ill off they themselv" s may hereafter be in the ease ol a drought of very long continuance. The Diet is still sitting, which gives general dissatisfaction, as the expense is, of course, great The number of representatives for the clergy, for instance, is about 50, lor the citizens nearly the same, and for the peasants rather more than 100. When we consider that each of these receive about 5s a day from his constituents, we cannot be surprised at their wishing for an end to that business. The King, however, declared that early in JVlay he would dissolve the Diet. His Majesty's ill health has, without doubt, conduced much to lengthen it. The Art of Writing is not general among the Turks; and when they are in love with a person to whom they cannot have easy access, they have a mode of writing their sentiments wiihout pen, ink, or paper, by the means of flowers, fruits, wood, ssilks, stuff's, and colours, of which they make a packet, each article having an allegorical sense : this packet they call a ted am. Those who employ this mode of communication have always a casket full of things to compose a setam. They have a dictionary, which they know by heart, of the allusions they wish to give by their flowers, &.c. Thus þÿ An ambret signifies, We are both of one mind. A piece of rose bush. 1 weep continually, but you deride my tears. A piece of cloth. I am tired with your importunities. A piece of canvass or buckram. We shall be together tomoirow. A piece ol silk. You have gained my mind, A looking glass. 1 am ready to sacrifice myself to you. A pistol. I love you very much. A grain of a raisin, some blue silk, a pea, a morsel ol sugar, and a piece of the wood of aloes, arrranged in certain order, from a billet doux to this purpose : þÿ " My heart, I am in love with you ; the pain which my love occasions me has nearly deprived me of my senses; my heart passionately desires you Give my disease the necessary remedy." a " short" joke A person complaining, at a tavern, of the sniallncss of some chops brought to table, a coffee room wag observed, " Probably the sheep was fed on short commons."

ISOTICK I hereby offer a REWARD of TWO THOUSAND-POUNDS to any person that will be the means of Discovering w here my Brother, THOMAS SMITH, is. lie is Ahsent since 1811. He went from an English School. Was then Eleven Years old, fair Haired, fair Complexion, Blue lives, Freckled He was born in the County of Limerick, in Ireland. Letters addressed to the l ast or H esf India Houses in London, will be forwarded to me. JANE BREW A. SMITH. Dated 23d of June, 183.').

The above is a copy of a Circular received hv His Excellency the Lieutenant Governor of this Colony, and by him forwaded to our Olfice for publication. Subjoined to the Circular is a Letter from Tomkins Brew, Esq., (husband ol Jane Brew, born Smith), detailing the particulars which ho had discovered regarding the disappearance of his Brother in Law. They arc briefly as follows : þÿ Thomas Smith was sent from Ireland to he educated under the care of the Reverend Henry Price, of Need wood Parsonage, near Litchfield, Staffordshire, where he remained for about a year and a half, when, being deceived into the belief that he was the natural son of his father, who he was informed had just died, leaving him wholly unprovided for, and that his only sister, the present Mrs. Brew , had also died at school, he was induced to join some other lads who had determined on seeking their fortunes in the West Indies, and with that view, engaged himself to an estate in Jamaica, belonging to Mr. Hall, of Holly Bush, in Staff irdshire Since this time nothing certain has been learned regarding him ; but there has been some teason to think that he might be heard of in some part of the parish ef St Andrew's in Jamaica. At the time Thomas Smith was spirited away from his country and his friends, his father was indeed dead ; but so far from leaving him destitute, lie had bequeathed to him an Estate in County Limerick worth Nine Hundred Pounds per annum, and Six Thousand Pounds in cash, besides Plate, Furniture,

Ate., with the proviso that if he died under age, the whole should devolve on his guardian, who was residuary legatee. From this proviso resulted the exile of Thomas Smith; the Guardian, in order to secure the reversion of this handsome property > having suborned .Mr. Price to stimulate the lad to leave his home, never to return. This nefarious transaction was not discovered until after Mr Brew's marriage with the sister of the missing youth, when the above facts were elicited by diligent enquiry. Mr. Brew's Address is TOM KI VS BREW, Esq., Chief Magistrate, Ennis, County Clare, Ireland.

The Circular which heads the above paragraph was published in the West Indies some two years ago, but failed in its object ; the additional particulars now furnished by Mr Brew may perhaps lead to a more successful result, especially if our Brethren of the Island Newspaper Press will forward the work of charity, by copying into their columns the : foregoing detail. þÿ Demeraia Royal Gazette, I August 13. Character of the Principal Nations of Europe. þÿ In religion, the German is sceptical ; the Englishman, devout; the Frenchman, zealous ; the Italian, ceremonious ; the .Spaniard, a bigot. In keeping his word, the German is faithful ; the Englishman, sale ; the Frenchman, giddy; the Italian, shutiling; the Spaniard, a cheat. In giving advice, the German is slow ; the Englishman, fearless ; the Frenchman, precipitate ; the Italian, nice ; the Spaniard, circumspect. In external appearance, the German is large; the Englishman, well made; the Frenchman, well looking; the Italian, of middle size; the Spaniard, awkward. In dress, the German is shabby ; the Englishman, costly ; the Frenchman, fickle ; the Italian, ragged ; the Spaniard, decent. In manners, the German is clownish; the Englishman, barbarous ; the Frenchman easy ; the Italian, polite; the Spaniard, proud. In keeping a secret, the German forgets what he has been told ; the Englishman conceals what he should divulge, and divulges what he should conceal ; the Frenchman tells every thing; ihe Indian is close; the Spaniard mysterious In canity, the German boasts little ; the Englishman despises all other nations; the Frenchman flat lers everybody; the Italian estimates cautiously ; the Spaniard is inditlerent. j In eating and drinking, the German is a drunkard ; the Englishman, gross and luscious ; the Frenchman, delicate; the Italian moderate; the Spaniard, penurious. in speaking, the German and Frenchman

speak badly, but write well ; the Englishman speaks ami writes well ; the Italian speaks well, writes much and well; the Spaniard speaks little, writes little, but well. Servants are companions in Germany ; obedient in England : masters in France ; respectful in Iialv; submissive in Spain. I lie women ai> housewives in Germany queens in England ; ladies in France ; captives in Italy : slaves in Spain. In courage, the German resembles a hear; the Englishman, a lion; the frenchman, an agio; the Italian, a lox ; and the Spaniard, a.i elephant. In the si lences, the German is a pedant ; the Englishman, a philosopher ; the Frenchman, a smatterer ; the Italian, a professor; me Spaniard a grave thinker. British Officers Abroad. þÿ It is a singular fact, and I look upon it as a degrading one, that the French officers while at Madrid made, in the ratio of five to one, more conquests than we did ! How is this to be accounted for? 'ihe British oflieers have the advantage of appearance; his exterior is fur before that of a Frenchman; his fortune, generally speaking, is ten times as great ; hut what of all this, if the one accommodates himself to the mantlets, nay the whims, of those he is thrown amongst, while the other, disregarding all forms, sticks to his national habits, struts about, and not only despises, hut lets it be seen that he despises, all lie meets, save those of his ow n nation.
